extracted.intended_audience: journalism students and newspaper reporters (learners/practitioners of news writing)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and checklist for analyzing and producing newspaper news and feature stories, covering forms, structure, style, typographical conventions, news values, sourcing, and special treatment for fires/accidents. Intended as a classroom/textbook rubric for student analysis of published items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-interest (constructive) feature
rubrics_metrics.description: The human interest element in the constructive type of story: the writer is able to make the emotional appeal to the readers that is particularly effective in accomplishing the purposes of this kind of story. Stories of this type may or may not have a summary lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such stories emphasize emotional appeal; may avoid summary lead; evaluate whether the human-interest element accomplishes the story's constructive purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entertaining feature story (literary ability)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the entertaining feature story that contains little or no news, the interest lies entirely in the manner in which the facts are told. The literary ability of the writer is here tested to the utmost, for a story is read only so far as it interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the writer's literary skill, narrative voice, and ability to sustain reader interest; story length should be determined by success at sustaining interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of discourse: narrative/descriptive/expository
rubrics_metrics.description: News stories in method are (1) narrative, (2) descriptive, (3) expository, or (4) any combination of these three forms of discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify which form(s) the story uses; many stories combine forms (e.g., narrate incidents, describe persons/places, explain causes/motives/results).

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative informative vs. narrative feature distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: In the purely informative news story that is narrative in form there is little suspense, because the essential facts are usually summarized in the beginning, or lead. In the narrative feature story, however, the interest is frequently sustained by the same devices that are used in fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether narrative devices create suspense or whether facts are presented up front; check for use of fiction techniques in features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description — suggestive or detailed
rubrics_metrics.description: Description in news stories may be either suggestive or detailed. The purpose in both kinds of description should be to convey to the reader impressions of sights, sounds, etc., as vivid as those the reporter himself experienced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether description conveys vivid impressions; in short pieces use suggestive touches; long pieces may contain considerable detail when warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exposition: simplicity and lucidity
rubrics_metrics.description: News stories are expository, as a whole or in part, whenever situations must be made clear by explaining motives, causes, results, and other phases of the news, or by summarizing speeches, reports, etc. Such exposition should always be as simple and lucid as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess clarity of explanation and avoidance of unnecessary complexity when explaining causes or summarizing material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure: beginning (lead) and body
rubrics_metrics.description: The structure of the news story is concerned with (1) the beginning, or lead, and (2) the body of the story. The informative story usually begins with a summary lead that answers Who? What? Where? When? Why? How?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether the lead answers the six basic questions; determine which of the following elements are included: persons, event, place, time, cause, significant circumstances; note if any element is 'featured' in place of prominence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Featured element in lead
rubrics_metrics.description: Any one of these elements of the news may be 'featured' in the place of prominence at the beginning of the story, although the time and the place are seldom played up in this way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether an element is intentionally featured and whether that choice serves the story's news value and reader interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature story openings (avoid summary lead)
rubrics_metrics.description: The story of entertainment or appeal usually avoids the summary lead by beginning in one of the ways common to fictitious narratives. In its beginning, its effort to sustain suspense, and its semblance of plot the human interest or feature story closely resembles the short story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For features, examine the opening technique: does it use scene-setting, anecdote, or fictional devices to hook readers rather than a summary lead?

rubrics_metrics.name: Body arrangement and repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: In the body of the story the details follow a logical order. The arrangement in narrative stories is usually chronological. Only such of the details summarized in the lead are repeated in the body of the story as are needed for clearness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess logical order (chronology for narrative), economy of repetition, and whether the ending sufficiently rounds out the story given space/makeup constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph and sentence analysis (unity, coherence, emphasis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysis of paragraphs and sentences should include: (1) the length of the paragraph and of the sentence; (2) the unity of thought in the sentence, and the unity of topic in the paragraph; (3) the coherence, or connection between the parts; and (4) the emphasis given to the important ideas by their position in sentence and paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate length, unity, coherence, and whether important ideas are emphasized by placement at sentence/paragraph beginnings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspaper paragraph length convention
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of the narrowness of the columns the newspaper paragraph must be comparatively short to avoid appearing heavy and uninviting. The typical newspaper paragraph contains from 36 to 76 words, whereas the average paragraph in ordinary prose is from 150 to 250 words in length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure average paragraph length against these conventions; consider visual readability in narrow columns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence construction and readability
rubrics_metrics.description: In sentence length, and in paragraph and sentence unity and coherence, the style of the news story does not differ from that of other prose. Involved constructions, long periodic sentences, and similar rhetorical devices, however, have no place in journalistic writing, because they tend to prevent rapid reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for simple, direct sentence constructions and avoidance of long periodic or involved rhetoric to enable rapid reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis by initial position
rubrics_metrics.description: The emphasis given to an important point by placing it at the beginning of a sentence or a paragraph, is a distinctive characteristic of newspaper style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether important points are positioned initially to catch the rapid reader's eye.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word choice and diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific words in original combinations are always preferable to colorless, general terms and trite phrases. Technical, scientific, and learned words should be avoided unless fully explained. Slang and colloquial expressions may be used when the tone of the story justifies them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate originality of diction, appropriateness of technical terms, and tasteful use (or avoidance) of slang relative to tone and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearness and movement
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearness, which is essential to rapid reading, depends upon the arrangement, the connection, and the expression of ideas. How brisk movement and steady progress can be secured is also worthy of notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge overall clarity and narrative movement; note techniques used to secure brisk pacing and steady progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor and pathos — tasteful use
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor and pathos are not infrequent in news stories, particularly in those of the feature and human interest type. The student should observe how humor may be effective without ridicule, buffoonery, or vulgarity, and how offensive facts may be presented in news stories without violating the canons of good taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether humorous or pathetic elements are used effectively and tastefully, without offence or sensationalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typographical style and consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Peculiarities in such details of typographical style as abbreviation, capitalization, hyphenation, and the use of numerical figures should be noted in each story and associated with the newspaper from which the story was taken, for each paper has a typographical style of its own. One style is as good as another, but it is essential that consistency be maintained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for house-style conventions and internal consistency; note use of boxes, bold-face, lists, market report forms, sports scores and other typographical devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: News values — context and audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions to analyze news values: In what paper was the story published? What are the policy and the character of the paper? How widely does the paper circulate? Does the paper appeal to a particular class of readers? Is the piece presented from that class's point of view? What, for the average reader, is the source of interest in the news? How much would the news interest the average reader? Was the space appropriate? What more significant phases might have been developed?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these questions to judge the story's newsworthiness relative to the paper's policy, circulation, and intended audience; evaluate angle, prominence, and space allocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of news (verification and origin)
rubrics_metrics.description: How did the news originate? Where was the first record of it probably made? By whom? What records and what persons may have been consulted in securing the news? What reference books or material may have been used in getting or in verifying the details of the story? What other possible sources might have been consulted?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess completeness of sourcing, likely first records, and whether adequate verification and background work were done.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of news gathering
rubrics_metrics.description: What evidence does the story give of the methods by which the news was obtained? Is there any evidence that the reporter or correspondent failed to get any of the important details of the piece of news?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for indications of interviews, eye-witness accounts, official records, and any gaps suggesting incomplete reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the story seem to be fair and unbiased? Is there evidence that any important facts were suppressed or that the story was colored to conform to the policy of the paper? Is the handling of the news constructive or destructive in its effect? What, if any, is the constructive purpose of the writer? Is the story so treated as to tempt the reader to imitate anti-social acts?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate impartiality, omissions, alignment with paper policy, potential social effects, and whether constructive aims (prevention, sympathy, reform) are present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type of story — detailed checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the primary purpose of the story to inform or to entertain? Is the story largely narrative and descriptive? Is it largely explanatory? Is it largely direct or indirect quotation? If narrative, is the order chronological? Is the narrative clear or confused? Does the narrative move slowly or briskly? Are eyewitness accounts used and are they direct or indirect? Are remarks and conversation of participants given? Is the description detailed or suggestive? Is there a striving for effect? If the story is that of a speech, report, etc., is the material arranged in logical order? Is much or little made of the personal or human interest element?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this multifaceted checklist to classify the story type and judge clarity, pace, sourcing, descriptive technique, handling of quotes, and human-interest treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure-of-story checklist (lead & body specifics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Has the story a summary lead or an unconventional beginning? Does the lead contain the essential facts concisely presented? Is the most striking detail played up as the feature in the first group of words of the opening sentence of the lead? What other element might have been featured? Is the lead proportionate in length to the whole story? How are the details arranged in the body? Is there any evidence that the story was cut down? Are the paragraphs closely connected? Is there unnecessary repetition? Could the arrangement of the details be improved?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these focused questions to evaluate lead effectiveness, balance, proportion, body arrangement, and editing/length issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph-level literary style checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: What is the average length of the paragraphs? Are any of the paragraphs too long or too short? Is each paragraph a unit? Are the details well arranged and closely connected in the paragraphs? Does the first group of words at the beginning of each paragraph attract the reader as his eye glances down the story? Could any of the paragraph beginnings be made more effective?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess paragraph unity, length appropriateness, internal arrangement, and effectiveness of paragraph openings for eye-scanning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence-level literary style checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: What is the average length of the sentences? Are any of the sentences too long or too short? Is the construction of each sentence evident in rapid reading? Is each sentence a unified expression of a closely related group of ideas? Are the parts of the sentences combined in firm, closely knit construction? Do the sentence beginnings attract the reader? Do any sentences trail off loosely into a succession of phrases and clauses? Is there variety in sentence length and sentence construction?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate sentence clarity, unity, rhythm, variety, and whether sentence openings provide immediate interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word-level checklist (diction and tone)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the style concise or wordy? Is the diction original or hackneyed? Is the style marked by many adjectives or by superlatives? Are the verbs specific and forcible? Is the diction too learned for the comprehension of the average rapid reader? Are words used idiomatically and accurately? Are slang and colloquial expressions found in the story? What is the effect of them? Is the diction in keeping with the tone of the story?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge concision, originality of diction, overuse of adjectives/superlatives, verb strength, appropriateness for rapid readers, idiomatic accuracy, and tone consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of style (overall readability and taste)
rubrics_metrics.description: Can the details of the story be easily comprehended in rapid reading; that is, is the style comparatively simple? Upon what does the general clearness depend? Is the movement slow or rapid? Is there any humor or pathos in the story? How is the humorous or the pathetic effect secured? Has the news possibilities for humorous or pathetic treatment that are not developed? Is the story in good taste?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess overall readability, sources of clearness, pacing, use and effect of humor/pathos, missed opportunities, and adherence to good taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typographical-style specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: What are the peculiarities of abbreviation, capitalization, hyphenation, and use of numerical figures? Is the typographical style consistent throughout the story? Are any details of the story given prominence by typographical devices? If so, why?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note house-style choices and typographical emphasis; consider whether typographical devices aid comprehension or distort emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fires and accidents — typical type and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Many newspaper reports of fires and accidents may be considered as typical examples of narrative and descriptive news stories of the purely informative type: essential facts are presented in a simple, direct, concise manner without any attempt to give greater interest than the facts themselves possess.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For fires/accidents, judge whether reporting is concise and factual; if human life is involved, note whether human-interest elements are added while preserving accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fires and accidents — constructive vs. sensational purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories of fires and accidents, particularly when fatalities occur, may be written so as to be either constructive or destructive in their influence. The constructive effect lies in emphasis upon elements that tend (1) to turn attention to preventive measures, (2) to create sympathy for victims, or (3) to inspire admiration for heroism. Stories that pander to ghastly and sensational phases have an unwholesome influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate emphasis on prevention, responsibility, sympathy, or heroism versus sensational, morbid focus; judge social impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of fires/accidents (narrative and sources)
rubrics_metrics.description: All types of fire and accident stories give opportunity for spirited narrative and vivid description. Possible means for lending life and interest include accounts of the disaster, either in direct or indirect quotation form, as secured by interviews with survivors and eye-witnesses, and conversation between persons involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for use of survivor/eyewitness interviews, direct/indirect quotes, and descriptive narrative that remains accurate and responsible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contents checklist for fires and accidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Among the important details to be considered in analyzing stories of unexpected occurrences are: (1) number of lives lost; (2) number of lives endangered; (3) names of dead and injured; (4) prominent persons and places involved; (5) character and extent of damage; (6) property threatened with damage or destruction; (7) cause and responsibility; (8) investigations; (9) preventive measures against recurrence of event; (10) probable or actual effects; (11) peculiar and unusual circumstances; (12) humorous and pathetic incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this checklist to ensure reporting includes all relevant factual particulars and to determine which detail should be played up in lead and prominence based on news value.
